idiom_name: Piscina<Job, Result> with typed run() over worker_threads
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds types, not a runtime, so the pool is Node's worker_threads or a browser Worker pool and what changes is the interface: Piscina ships its own types and models tasks as run<T>(task): Promise<T>, so task inputs and results are checked at the call site, while node:worker_threads itself needs @types/node and usually a small typed wrapper (env, transferList and SharedArrayBuffer are all typed). The same rules as JavaScript apply - workers exist for CPU-bound work because the event loop already handles I/O - and the typed library is preferable to re-implementing queue bookkeeping by hand.
pitfalls: Types do not cross the thread boundary at runtime: structured-clone semantics still apply, so the worker must validate what it receives.
Worker entry points are separate modules: bundlers need them emitted as their own chunks (new URL(..., import.meta.url) is the portable form).
A typed pool library can still be misconfigured (maxThreads, idleTimeout, queue bounds); types say nothing about sizing or backpressure.

variants.name: Typed browser Web Worker pool
variants.idiom_name: typed generic pool wrapper over browser Worker instances
variants.implementation_notes: In the browser the pool is a fixed set of Worker instances fed through postMessage, and TypeScript's role is a type-safe message protocol: declare a request/response union per worker and wrap the pool in a generic run<Req, Res>(req: Req): Promise<Res> that hides queueing, navigator.hardwareConcurrency sizing and terminate()-on-failure. Use the lib.dom typings; shared-memory parallelism with SharedArrayBuffer and Atomics additionally requires the page to be cross-origin isolated.
pitfalls: The DOM typings do not model the message protocol: a generic wrapper is what keeps requests and responses honest across the boundary.
postMessage is structured clone, so class instances, DOM nodes and functions do not survive - send plain data.
terminate() bypasses cleanup; a typed API that hides it can still leak workers if tasks are never cancelled.
